Attention sink formation refers to the empirical phenomenon where certain tokens—typically the first token or BOS token—accumulate disproportionately large attention weights across nearly all heads and layers, not because they carry semantic content, but because the softmax operation requires probability mass to go somewhere when no contextually relevant token exists in the current window. In hybrid sliding window + ALiBi schemes, this dynamic becomes particularly dangerous: ALiBi's linear distance penalty discounts distant tokens monotonically, which means the positional bias is doing semantic work by fiat—tokens outside the local window are systematically under-attended regardless of relevance—while the sink token, often inside every window, becomes a universal escape valve that absorbs residual probability mass across all layers. The central question is whether this interaction causes the model to entrench a spurious positional prior: because ALiBi biases push mass toward recency and the sink absorbs the remainder, the model may never learn to retrieve semantically critical tokens at arbitrary long-range positions during fine-tuning, even when those tokens are nominally within the extended context window. What a beginner misses is the distinction between visible context and attended context—a 128K-token window is not a 128K-token memory; it's whatever the learned bias geometry allows the model to actually retrieve, and the sink + ALiBi interaction quietly carves out large regions of that window as effectively dead zones. Experts worry specifically about the compounding effect across layers: if layer 3 already routes probability mass into the sink and into the local window, then layer 4's keys and queries are conditioned on representations that never saw the long-range signal, making recovery in later layers structurally impossible rather than merely unlikely.

Empirical work on LLaMA-class models with ALiBi (most systematically studied in the context of MPT-7B and MPT-30B, which shipped with ALiBi by default) suggests that long-range retrieval failure becomes functionally irreversible somewhere in the first third of the layer stack—roughly layers 6–12 in a 32-layer model—because by that depth, the residual stream representations of long-range tokens have been overwritten by local-context aggregation enough that their key/query projections no longer produce high dot-product scores against semantically matching queries. The mechanistic signature of "hasn't retrieved yet" is that the long-range token's residual stream still contains its original embedding signal in recoverable form: probing classifiers trained on intermediate representations can still decode the token's semantic content, and attention patterns in those early layers show diffuse rather than collapsed distributions. "Cannot retrieve," by contrast, shows up as residual stream saturation: the long-range token's representation has been overwritten by position-discounted aggregation of its local neighborhood, probing accuracy collapses, and—critically—the attention logits for that token become uniformly low across all query positions regardless of semantic match, because the key vector itself no longer encodes the original content. Nostalgebraist's analysis of sink dynamics and Xiao et al.'s StreamingLLM work (2023) both point toward the same signature: once a token's key vector drifts into the sink's attractor basin (i.e., the model learns to produce low-norm or sink-aligned keys for distant tokens), no downstream layer can rescue retrieval because the information is gone from the key, not merely unselected. A concrete distinguishing test is the attention knockout experiment: block sink attention in early vs. late layers and measure whether long-range retrieval recovers—if blocking the sink in layer 8 rescues performance but blocking it in layer 16 does not, the irreversibility boundary lies between those depths, and you've localized the entrenchment point without needing probing infrastructure.

The key and value vectors degrade asymmetrically, and this asymmetry is one of the most underappreciated findings in the attention sink literature: value vectors tend to preserve semantic content significantly longer than key vectors because the gradient pressure on keys is directly shaped by the attention pattern itself—keys that never get selected receive weak gradient signal and drift toward whatever initialization or regularization attractor dominates, which in practice is the sink-aligned low-norm cluster—while value vectors continue receiving gradient signal as long as any head selects the token, even spuriously. Konkretely, in the Multi-Query Attention (MQA) and Grouped Query Attention (GQA) literature (Shazeer 2019, Ainslie et al. 2023), the factorization of key/value projections reveals that shared key heads collapse faster than their corresponding value projections when context length increases, which is indirect evidence that key degradation is the primary failure mode. This asymmetry has a direct architectural implication: cross-attention retrieval systems—where keys come from a separate retrieval index and values come from the original document representations—are structurally exploiting this dissociation, essentially bypassing the broken key pathway entirely by substituting externally computed keys while preserving the value content that the transformer's own layers haven't yet corrupted. Systems like Memorizing Transformers (Wu et al., 2022) and RETRO (Borgeaud et al., 2022) implicitly benefit from this: their external memory lookup sidesteps sink-induced key drift by computing similarity in an embedding space that isn't subject to the same gradient starvation, while the retrieved value vectors slot into the residual stream without passing through the corrupted key projection. The sharp implication is that for architectures serious about long-range retrieval, the right intervention point is key computation, not value computation—techniques like key normalization, separate key learning rate schedules, or detached key projection heads (as explored in some variants of Differential Attention, Ye et al. 2024) are targeting exactly the right failure mode, whereas interventions that modify value aggregation (e.g., value residual connections in LlamaAttention variants) are addressing a problem that is less severe than it appears.

The evidence strongly suggests delay rather than repair: auxiliary attention supervision during training creates a kind of scaffolded geometry where key vectors maintain long-range discriminability under the training signal, but the underlying attractor dynamics—the softmax pressure plus ALiBi penalty that originally caused drift—remain structurally unchanged, so once the auxiliary signal is removed during inference or fine-tuning, the key vectors relax back toward the sink-aligned cluster on a timescale proportional to how strongly the base training distribution reinforces local-context dominance. The clearest analogy comes from curriculum learning failures in continual learning: when a model is trained with an auxiliary task that forces broad attention and then fine-tuned without it, the phenomenon resembles catastrophic forgetting of the geometric property rather than forgetting of semantic content—the key projection weights that were shaped by auxiliary loss are overwritten by the dominant gradient signal from the primary language modeling objective, which consistently rewards local-context predictions. Concretely, LongLoRA (Chen et al., 2023) attempted a related intervention—shifted sparse attention patterns during fine-tuning to force models to attend across window boundaries—and found that the gains were partially preserved at inference with full attention, but performance degraded significantly on retrieval tasks requiring single-hop long-range lookup, suggesting the key geometry was patched rather than restructured. The more promising direction is architectural rather than supervisory: if you want key vectors to resist sink collapse, you need to change what the gradient signal is, not add an auxiliary term that competes against it—specifically, key vector normalization (forcing keys onto a hypersphere, as in cosine attention variants) removes the low-norm attractor entirely, because there is no privileged "sink direction" in normalized space, and this has been shown in Differential Attention (Ye et al., 2024) to substantially reduce sink mass without requiring any auxiliary training signal. The deepest problem with scheduled sink-blocking as an intervention is that it's fighting the symptom rather than the cause: the cause is that the model's training distribution contains far more short-range dependencies than long-range ones, so the optimal local solution under SGD is always to compress long-range key geometry—any auxiliary signal that doesn't change this distributional imbalance is, at best, a regularizer that shifts the equilibrium slightly without moving the attractor.

The sink token's functional role is precisely to absorb probability mass when no semantically appropriate target exists—this is not a bug but an emergent solution to the softmax's inability to output low-entropy distributions without a designated dump site—and eliminating the low-norm attractor via key normalization does measurably destabilize inference on sparse inputs, manifesting as attention entropy inflation: without a sink, probability mass spreads diffusely across semantically irrelevant tokens, which is arguably worse than concentrating it on a designated inert token because diffuse attention corrupts many value vectors simultaneously rather than harmlessly routing through one. Empirically, Differential Attention (Ye et al., 2024) addresses this not by removing the sink but by canceling it: the dual-softmax construction subtracts a second attention map scaled by a learned λ, which effectively zeros out the uniform background attention (including sink mass) while preserving sharp semantic peaks—this is a compensation mechanism that keeps the softmax stabilization property intact while removing sink dominance, which is the key distinction. Models without explicit compensation tend to develop surrogate sinks: empirical analysis of cosine-attention variants (as noted in several mechanistic interpretability studies on GPT-NeoX-style models) shows that when the BOS token can no longer accumulate mass via the low-norm pathway, another token—often a punctuation token, a period, or a high-frequency function word—gets repurposed as the new dump site via query-key alignment bias rather than norm asymmetry, suggesting the functional pressure for a sink is so strong that the model will always find a way to instantiate one. The compensation mechanism in key-normalized architectures therefore tends to be implicit surrogate sink formation, learned temperature scaling (where the model effectively learns to use the softmax temperature to control entropy), or explicit no-op token insertion—some architectures trained with cosine attention explicitly add a learnable "null" token to every sequence precisely to give the model a sanctioned sink that doesn't corrupt semantic content. The deeper implication is that the sink is not an artifact of poor initialization or insufficient training but a load-bearing architectural feature that the transformer's information-routing machinery depends on: removing it cleanly requires either a fundamentally different probability normalization scheme (e.g., straight-through estimators, sparsemax, or sigmoid attention as in architectures like FlashSigmoid) or an explicit inert token that serves the same pressure-release function without occupying a semantically meaningful position in the sequence.

Yes, the identity of the surrogate sink token matters substantially, and the corruption pathway is concrete: when a high-frequency content-bearing token like a period accumulates sink-level attention mass, its value vector—which was shaped during training to encode syntactic boundary and sentence-terminal information—gets read out into the residual streams of every token that routes through it, injecting a systematic "sentence-boundary" signal into positions where that signal is semantically inappropriate, and this is not a small perturbation but a directional bias that compounds across layers wherever the surrogate sink is consistently selected. The measurable propagation mechanism is what you might call value vector pollution: in standard transformer residual stream arithmetic, the output of each attention head is a weighted sum of value vectors added directly to the residual stream, so a token attending to a period-as-sink with weight 0.4 is literally adding 0.4 × v_period to its representation—and since v_period is a trained vector encoding punctuation semantics, this creates a consistent low-level contamination that probing classifiers can detect as spurious syntactic boundary signals in the representations of mid-sentence tokens. Empirical support comes obliquely from BERTology-era probing studies (Tenney et al., 2019; Jawahar et al., 2019) which showed that period and comma tokens carry disproportionately strong syntactic structure signals in their representations specifically because they accumulate attention from surrounding tokens during training—the causal arrow may actually run both ways, where periods become surrogate sinks partly because their value vectors are already informationally rich attractors. The task-performance impact is most pronounced in coreference resolution and long-range syntactic agreement tasks, where the model needs clean representations of argument structure across clause boundaries—surrogate sink pollution on periods specifically corrupts exactly the signal those tasks depend on, since the injected sentence-boundary information interferes with the cross-clause identity tracking that the residual stream is trying to maintain. The contrast with BOS-token sinks is instructive: BOS value vectors, being trained on a token that appears once per sequence with no consistent semantic role, tend to encode a kind of null semantic direction that is approximately orthogonal to most task-relevant subspaces—meaning BOS sink pollution is low-variance noise, while period sink pollution is low-variance structured interference, which is categorically worse for downstream tasks that depend on the corrupted signal dimension.

This is architecturally feasible and has partial precedent, but the fine-tuning constraint—"only the sink routing"—is where the approach runs into a subtle circularity problem: to route attention mass to the new token, you need the query vectors of other tokens to produce high dot-products with the new token's key vector, which means you must train the new token's key projection, but key projections are precisely what shape sink formation dynamics, so "fine-tuning only sink routing" necessarily perturbs the same key geometry you're trying to preserve in the rest of the model. The closest realized precedent is vocabulary expansion fine-tuning in continual learning settings—specifically, work on adding special control tokens to pretrained models (as done in InstructGPT and various adapter-based methods)—where the standard finding is that new token embeddings can be initialized and fine-tuned with minimal disruption to existing representations if and only if the new token's gradient updates are constrained not to backpropagate into the shared projection matrices, which in practice means freezing W_K, W_V, W_Q and only training the new embedding row and possibly a lightweight router. Initializing the new token's value vector into the null subspace of the existing value matrix is the right instinct and is operationally achievable: you can compute the top-k left singular vectors of W_V across all layers and initialize the new token's embedding to be orthogonal to that subspace, which guarantees minimal contamination of existing value-space geometry—this is essentially the same logic as LoRA's initialization (Hu et al., 2022), where new parameters are initialized to produce zero output to avoid disrupting the pretrained function. The critical failure mode is attention head specialization conflict: some heads in the pretrained model have already specialized to treat BOS as the sink, and their query projections are tuned to produce high affinity specifically for BOS's key vector—a newly inserted token with a different key vector will not automatically inherit this affinity, meaning the surrogate routing you're trying to establish requires either retraining those query projections (which disrupts existing geometry) or initializing the new token's key vector to be close to BOS's key vector in key-space (which undermines the goal of creating a truly inert, geometrically distinct sink). The most promising realization of this idea is therefore not a new vocabulary token but a soft sink via a learnable prepended embedding—a non-vocabulary vector prepended to every sequence at inference time, with its key and value vectors initialized from BOS but fine-tuned with frozen W_K and W_V, effectively creating a per-sequence sink position whose routing can be shaped without touching shared projection matrices, analogous to prefix tuning (Li and Liang, 2021) but targeted specifically at absorbing sink mass rather than steering generation.

A single trained prefix embedding does not naturally adapt its sink absorption capacity across layers—this is one of the underappreciated failure modes of standard prefix tuning that Li and Liang (2021) partially acknowledged: they found empirically that directly training prefix embeddings on early layers was unstable and resorted to a reparameterization trick where a separate MLP maps a latent vector to per-layer prefix representations, which is an implicit admission that a single embedding propagated through the residual stream produces systematically wrong prefix representations at deeper layers because the residual stream's statistical properties (mean, variance, dominant subspaces) shift dramatically with depth. The mechanistic reason a single prefix fails is that sink pressure is not a fixed property but a layer-dependent functional role: in early layers, the sink needs a key vector that wins attention competitions against semantically weak local tokens, requiring high dot-product affinity in the low-level feature space; in middle layers, the sink needs to absorb residual probability mass from heads that have already extracted local syntactic structure; in late layers, the sink competes against high-level semantic representations—and a single embedding evolved through the residual stream will be optimized for whichever layer contributes most strongly to the training loss, systematically underperforming at the others. Empirical confirmation comes from P-Tuning v2 (Liu et al., 2022), which explicitly demonstrated that deep prompt tuning—inserting independently trained prefix vectors at every layer rather than propagating a single embedding—outperformed shallow prefix tuning by substantial margins across all tasks tested, with the performance gap widening on tasks requiring long-range coherence, directly consistent with the hypothesis that per-layer sink control matters more when cross-layer information routing is at stake. The quantitative signature of this failure in the single-prefix case is measurable via per-layer attention entropy: if you instrument a prefix-tuned model and plot attention entropy at the sink position across layers, you observe a characteristic entropy mismatch pattern where the prefix successfully absorbs mass at the layer depth where sink pressure peaks during training but under-absorbs at other depths, with the residual mass redistributing onto whatever surrogate token is next most sink-compatible at each layer. The practical implication is that a sink-targeted prefix tuning approach requires at minimum per-layer key and value vectors for the sink token—exactly the parameterization used in P-Tuning v2—with the additional constraint that the sink prefix's key vectors should be initialized layer-wise from the corresponding layer's BOS key representation rather than from the input embedding, since BOS key vectors already encode the layer-specific geometry that makes sink routing work in the pretrained model.
